name: Proof of Concept
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Proving the Point Without Proving Too Much: What a Good Blockchain PoC Actually Tests
lesson.summary: A proof of concept is a small, time-boxed technical test of one specific, falsifiable question, not a business validation or a production trial, and defining pass or fail criteria before starting is what separates a useful PoC from PoC purgatory.
lesson.body:
Once a technology evaluation makes a reasoned case that blockchain might solve a real problem, the next step is not to build the production system. It is to test the narrowest, riskiest technical assumption the case depends on, cheaply and quickly, before committing serious resources. That narrow technical test is a proof of concept, and the discipline of keeping it narrow is exactly what makes it useful.

A good PoC answers one specific, falsifiable question, stated in advance: can we write and read a transaction across these three organizations' nodes with latency under a defined threshold; can this specific smart contract logic correctly enforce this specific business rule; can this consensus configuration handle this specific transaction volume. It typically runs on a small number of nodes, often on a single team's infrastructure or a shared testnet, using synthetic or sample data rather than real customer or transaction data, and over a short, fixed timeframe measured in weeks rather than months. Critically, a PoC is not a business validation. It is not designed to test whether stakeholders will adopt the system, whether the consortium's governance model will hold up, or whether the economics work at scale. Those are pilot program questions, covered in the next chapter, and conflating them with the PoC's narrower technical question is one of the most common design mistakes teams make.

The most common failure mode is not a PoC that fails. It is a PoC that never really tests anything and just sits there, sometimes called PoC purgatory: a demo that technically works on a laptop, gets shown in a few meetings, generates enthusiasm, and then never progresses to a pilot or a decision to stop, because it was never built around a clear, falsifiable question in the first place. Teams fall into this by choosing a PoC that only demonstrates what they already knew would work, avoiding the genuinely uncertain question that mattered, or by never defining what result would count as a failure. A PoC that cannot fail was not testing anything; it was a demo wearing the label of an experiment.

Avoiding that trap starts with writing down, before any code is built, exactly what result will count as a pass and what result will count as a fail, and getting the relevant stakeholders identified through the stakeholder analysis process to agree to those criteria in advance, when everyone is still reasoning from evidence rather than from sunk cost. It also means resisting the temptation to expand scope mid-flight; a PoC that keeps absorbing new features to keep stakeholders excited is drifting away from being a sharp technical test and toward being an unofficial, unbudgeted pilot. Organizational challenges covered earlier in this course, competitive distrust between consortium members, unresolved cost allocation, legacy integration debt, are almost never fully visible at PoC scale, which is exactly why a PoC succeeding is evidence about the technology and not yet evidence that the whole project will succeed. A team that treats a passed PoC as proof the hard organizational work is done is setting up the pilot that follows to be the place those deferred problems finally surface.
